message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge a security deposit, but it must be returned within 30 days after you move out, unless you give written notice of intent to stay.
• The deposit can only be used for unpaid rent, damages beyond normal wear, or cleaning if the lease specifies it. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection checklist.
• Take photos or videos of the unit when you move in and out. | | **Habitability** | • Texas law requires landlords to keep the premises in a habitable condition (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, structural safety).
• The landlord must repair any major defects that affect health or safety. | • Report problems in writing (email or letter) and keep a copy.
• If repairs are not made within a reasonable time, you may withhold rent or pursue a repair‑and‑deduct remedy (see below). | | **Repair‑and‑Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to fix a major problem, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from your rent, provided you give the landlord written notice and keep receipts. | • Document the issue, send a written notice, and keep receipts.
• The deduction cannot exceed the actual cost of the repair. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable (not punitive). | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re having trouble. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party can terminate a month‑to‑month lease with 30 days’ written notice.
• For a fixed‑term lease, you must follow the lease’s termination clause or risk forfeiting the security deposit. | • Provide written notice (email or letter) and keep a copy. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlords must not interfere with your peaceful use of the property.
• They cannot enter without notice (except in emergencies). | • Landlords must give at least 24 hours’ notice before entering, unless it’s an emergency. | | **Privacy** | • Landlords cannot enter the unit without notice, except for emergencies. | • Keep a log of any visits and ask for a written notice if you suspect unauthorized entry. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected classes. | • If you suspect discrimination, file a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the Texas eviction procedure: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment, 30‑day notice for lease termination).
• If you fail to comply, the landlord can file an unlawful detainer action in court. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• If you receive an eviction notice, consider contacting a tenant‑rights group or attorney. | | **Rent Control** | • Texas has no statewide rent‑control laws. | • Rent increases must be in accordance with the lease or a new lease agreement. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. | • Verify utility responsibilities before signing. | | **Subletting / Assignment** | • Many leases allow subletting or assignment with landlord approval. | • Get written permission before subletting. | | **Maintenance of Common Areas** | • Landlords must maintain common areas (hallways, stairwells, elevators) in a safe condition. | • Report hazards promptly. | | **Landlord’s Right to Inspect** | • Landlords may inspect the unit for maintenance or safety reasons, but must give reasonable notice (usually 24 hours). | • Keep a record of inspections. | | **Legal Remedies** | • If the landlord violates your rights, you can:
1. File a complaint with the Texas Attorney General’s Office or local housing agency.
2. Seek a court order (e.g., for repairs or to stop harassment).
3. Claim damages or recover withheld rent. | • Keep all documentation (emails, texts, receipts, photos). | ### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Understand the terms, notice periods, and responsibilities. 2. **Document the Unit** – Photos/videos at move‑in and move‑out. 3. **Keep Written Records** – All communications with the landlord (emails, letters, texts). 4. **Know the Notice Requirements** – 24‑hour notice for entry, 30‑day notice for termination. 5. **Report Problems Promptly** – In writing, with a copy for yourself. 6. **Know Your Eviction Rights** – Understand the notice types and timelines. 7. **Seek Help if Needed** – Tenant‑rights groups, legal aid, or the Texas Attorney General’s Office. --- #### Resources - **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division**: [https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/consumer-protection](https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/consumer-protection) - **Texas Commission on Human Rights**: [https://www.tchra.org/](https://www.tchra.org/) - **Texas Legal Services Center**: [https://www.texaslegalservices.org/](https://www.texaslegalservices.org/) - **Local Tenant‑Rights Organizations** – Search online for “tenant rights Texas” in your city. If you have a specific issue (e.g., a dispute over a security deposit, a repair that hasn’t been fixed, or an eviction notice), let me know and I can give more tailored guidance.
